en: The First Fascicle of the Mahāyāna *Vajramukuṭamaṇi-bodhisattva-caryā-prakaraṇa*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantārthacintin addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how is it so?"
The Bodhisattva practices and awakens to this samādhi.
The Buddha said, "Good son,
that which is without awakening or entry is called awakening and entry."
"It should also be as that which I realized and entered upon when I was cultivating bodhi.
The Bodhisattva Universal Contemplation of Meaning addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, what is the realization and entry cultivated by the Tathāgata?"
"I only pray that you will explain it.
The Buddha said, "Good son,
in the past there was a king named Vajramukuṭamaṇi."
While staying in a tranquil grove,
he sat cross-legged and contemplated with right mindfulness.
While dwelling in this manner:
To the right of his seat, a great lotus flower suddenly appeared.
This exquisite flower was composed of various precious gems;
its stalk was made of firm sandalwood encircled by nāgas.
Jāmbūnada gold forms its petals;
maṇi jewels form its filaments;
and kiṃśuka gems form its pericarp.
At that time, upon the most excellent lotus pedestal made of various jewels,
Prince Siddhārtha was suddenly born through transformation;
he sat cross-legged and arose with serene composure.
Descending from the lotus pedestal, he sat upon his right knee.
At that time, King Vajramukuṭamaṇi felt great joy and affection for Prince Siddhārtha.
Then, eighty-four thousand princes,
together with him, went to where that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Sūryaprabharāja, the Jewel-Mountain of the Buddha-Dharmadhātu, was residing.
Having heard and received the true Dharma,
and having heard this Samādhi of the Dharma-realm’s Silk Topknot and the Heart Chapter of Vajra Tathāgata,
they attained the five supernormal powers.
What is called the *samādhi* of the Dharma-realm Silk Topknot and the Heart of Vajra Tathāgata?
At that time, the Tathāgata Dharmadhātu-maṇi-parvata-sūryaprabha-rāja...
I shall now expound it for you:
namely, these syllables of Kīla, syllables of Vajra,
syllables of Dharma, and syllables of Mudrā.
The phrase of principle, the phrase of correspondence,
the phrase of secrecy, the phrase of retention,
the phrase of service, and the phrase of transformation.
The phrases of swift movement, the phrases of rapidity,
the phrases of manifestation, and the phrases of vidyā-mantras—
having thus spoken these phrases of this chapter.
It binds all Māras.
The *kīla* binding seal and the binding phrases—
these and all other such phrases entirely enter the phrase of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
It is without dispute or contention;
this is called the Samādhi of the Dharma-realm Silk Topknot and the Heart of Vajra Tathāgata.
It was expounded by that Tathāgata Sūryaprabhā-rāja of the Dharma-realm Maṇi Mountain.
"Good son, do you know this?
That world which was formerly called 'Jeweled Gold and Silver' is now this city of Laṅkā on Mount Malaya."
This world, composed of mani jewels, gold, and silver,
is the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Sūryaprabharāja, the Mani-jewel Mountain of the Dharma-realm.
Noble son, this is the Great King Vajraśekhara-maṇi-ratna.
In the past, in the world-system of the Tathāgata Sūryaprabharāja, which was composed of mani-jewels, gold, and silver,
he served as a universal monarch (cakravartin) over a thousand worlds.
Could this have been anyone else?
He is none other than the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
Good son, this Great King Crest-Jewel was a wheel-turning monarch within that buddha-field.
He had ten billion sons.
Could they be anyone else?
They are none other than the bodhisattvas who have come from the ten directions here today.
This was all for the sake of hearing the *Dharmadhātu-paṭṭacūḍā-vajratathāgata-hṛdaya-varga-samādhi-dharma*.
Good son, you should know this.
At that time, Prince Sarvasiddha possessed twenty-eight marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
All shall attain accomplishment.
Why is this? My very body is Prince Siddhārtha.
Long ago, within the Garden of Sublime Sound at the palace of King Śikhicūḍa, I...
While the king sat upright in right mindfulness and contemplation,
he was suddenly born by transformation upon a precious lotus pedestal made of dragon-firm sandalwood and *candana-jinśuka* to his right.
He immediately went to the presence of the Tathāgata Sūryaprabharāja, the Mountain of Maṇi Jewels of the Dharma-realm of that Buddha,
and there he heard the dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Dharma-realm Silk Topknot and the Heart Chapter of the Vajra Tathāgata.
From that time onward,
I have served and made offerings to immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas.
Having heard the "Chapter on the Heart of Vajra Tathāgata" from the *Dharmadhātu-paṭṭa-veṇī*,
he has never forgotten it since that time.
Throughout immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
by the power of samādhi, they constantly maintain mindfulness;
within a single kalpa, they can recollect a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand kalpas.
I also remember and have never forgotten;
I remember the kalpa of formation and I also remember the kalpa of destruction.
I also recollect the intermediate eons of formation and destruction,
even up to hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of eons.
They also constantly bring to mind one Tathāgata; from that,
they bring to mind a hundred Tathāgatas, a thousand Tathāgatas, and a hundred thousand Tathāgatas.
They also constantly keep in mind as many Tathāgatas as are unspeakably unspeakable, even up to koṭis of nayutas of Tathāgatas.
In the presence of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
he has already obtained the Dharma-gate of the Vajra-Tathāgata’s Heart Chapter, known as the Dharma-realm Silk Topknot.
He never forgot it.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning,
spoke these verses:
I recall in past ages, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas,
seeing various pure lands adorned with oceans of gold and jewels,
ruled by a king of pure maṇi lands named Vajra-śikhin.
Possessing great sovereign power, he rules over a thousand worlds, even up to ten thousand worlds; none can surpass him.
Endowed with a thousand billion sons, he is able to destroy all enemies.
All were endowed with the twenty-eight marks of a great man;
they attended upon the Great King at court.
Within the Prince’s Nāyuta Garden, the ponds and pavilions were all magnificent and beautiful.
Adorned with all manner of precious ornaments, I offer them to the Lamps of the World,
the Tathāgatas present before me; I universally entreat the Great Teacher of Universal Vision, who is the foremost of all.
I personally attended and served him for the sake of hearing the True Dharma.
Next there was the Buddha Samantabhadra; next, the Buddha Puṣpadīpa;
next, the Buddha Vajradīpa; and next, the Buddha Mahādīpa.
Next there was the Most Excellent Lamp; next, the Buddha Dharma-Lamp;

Next is the Buddha Brahmasthāna; next is the Buddha Manuṣyaloka;
next is the Buddha Devendra; next is the Buddha Mahāyāna;
next is the Buddha Varamati. O Son of the Buddha, such are the names of these Tathāgatas.
Appearing in the world during each of those eons,
I served them all as if they were reliquaries or shrines,
solely out of my aspiration for this samādhi.
O Son of the Buddha, after further passing beyond those kalpas,
and again passing beyond a number of kalpas equal to the atoms within ten unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
there was a Buddha during a great kalpa.
He was named Tathāgata Maṇiparvataraviprabhāsarāja.
When he first appeared, I personally attended upon him for the sake of seeking this samādhi.
Next, there was the Tathāgata named Suvarṇaparvataśikha;
next, there was the Tathāgata named Dharmadhātumaṇivajraparvatāgrapradīparāja.
I also served them.
Next, there was another Tathāgata named Suvarṇaparvata-maṇiśikhara-sūryacūḍa,
whom I also served. Following that,
there was another Tathāgata named Vimalamaṇipradīpa.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Dharmadhātu-maṇi-vajra-śikhara-dīpa;
next, the Tathāgata Vajrarāja;
and next, the Tathāgata Gaganasama-maṇi-vajra.
Next, there was the Tathāgata named Puṇyaparvata-vajra,
whom I also served.
Next, there was the Tathāgata named Gotradīparāja.
Next was the Tathāgata Vimalavajrapradīpahasta-rāja;
next, the Tathāgata Vajrapradīpa;
and next, there was the Tathāgata Vajra.
Next, I also served the Tathāgata Vimalaprabhāvajra.
Following that was the Tathāgata Vīryavajra.
I also served him.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Kuliśa-vajra;
next, there was the Tathāgata Vajra-śikhin.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Kūṇaṃdhara-vajra;
next, the Tathāgata Vajragarbha;
and next, the Tathāgata Vajracandra.
I also served him.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Sāgaracandra;
next, there was the Tathāgata Aṅkuśavajra.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Samantamaṇivajracūḍa;
next, the Tathāgata Nārāyaṇavajra;
and next, the Tathāgata Vimalacandra.
Next there was the Tathāgata Dharmarāga;
next there was the Tathāgata Dharmatattva;
next there was the Tathāgata Dharmasvara.

next was the Tathāgata Good Fragrance.
Next was the Tathāgata Suprabha;
next was the Tathāgata Samantagarbha;
next was the Tathāgata Samantaśīrṣa.
Next there was the Tathāgata Candrasūrya;
next, the Tathāgata Sārthavāha;
and next, the Tathāgata Suvarṇaparvatejaprabha.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Sound-Light;
next, the Tathāgata Ground of Certain Non-Abiding;
and next, the Tathāgata Victorious Banner.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Manifesting Majestic Radiance;
next, the Tathāgata Great Flame;
and next, the Tathāgata Jewel Flame.
Next, there was the Tathāgata Mahātathāgata;
next, the Tathāgata Sūryacandraprabha;
and next, the Tathāgata Candanagandhābhyudgata.
Next there was the Tathāgata Siṃhadhvaja;
next there was the Tathāgata Padmaprabha;
and next there was the Tathāgata Suvarṇaniyatamaṇiparvatejoravitejarāja.
I have served all such Tathāgatas.
Son of good family, in this way, for the sake of seeking this Dharma-gate,
I have recollected them for one kalpa, and I have recollected them for a hundred kalpas.
He recollects a thousand eons; he also recollects a hundred thousand eons.
He recollects the eon of formation, he also recollects the eon of destruction, and he also recollects the intermediate period between the eon of formation and the eon of destruction.
I also remember as many as unspeakably unspeakable eons of formation and destruction,
and hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of eons.
"Good son, I also remember a hundred buddhas; I remember a thousand buddhas and a hundred thousand buddhas;
even up to unspeakable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of buddhas, I remember them all."
In the presence of these Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
this Dharma-realm silk-turban *Vajratathāgatacittavarga-samādhi* arose.
Having heard them there,
I have made offerings to and served them all;
I shall never forget this samādhi.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha,
if there are good men or good women whose three karmas are pure, they should aspire to and seek this samādhi.
If there are those who delight in the meaning of clarity, or in the characteristics of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles;
those who love the meaning of the Dharma, or who love eloquence;
those who delight in supernormal powers, or who delight in renown.
Those who delight in physical beauty and those who love incantations should uphold,
make offerings to, and widely expound this samādhi for others.
If there are members of the fourfold assembly— monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen— [who do so].
Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others,
including Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors.
One should aspire to this. Why?
Because this dharma-gate impartially gathers in and embraces suffering sentient beings.
Like a treasure trove within the earth,
he is one who delights in the wealth of the Dharma;
he is a great radiance that illuminates those fallen into the darkness of ignorance.
This is the great flash of lightning for those who wish to enter the path to nirvāṇa;
this dharma-gate is the wisdom of the foolish.
O Son of the Buddha, such is this dharma-gate.
Entering into all the teachings of the Buddhas:
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if one were to take a portion consisting of the three-thousandfold world system filled with the seven treasures.
If there is anyone who hears this Dharma-gate,
the accumulation of their roots of goodness and the fruit of their merit will be far superior to that;
let alone the case of dividing the seven treasures of a trichiliocosm as gifts.
If there were sentient beings of the six realms in as many trichiliocosm great thousandfold world systems as there are sands in the Ganges River,
and if someone possessed such courageous power and majesty as to bring that realm of sentient beings to fulfillment.
He provided them with all the requisites for their enjoyment as they desired.
He continued to honor and revere them for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of years.
After all those sentient beings had attained parinirvāṇa, [he remained].
Furthermore, one should construct for them a sublime stupa made of the seven precious gems;
such merit and virtue will be immeasurable and boundless.
If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate, [they shall likewise attain it].
The merit surpasses that [of the former].
Let alone the matter of all sentient beings in the six realms of existence, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
suppose, for instance, within a trichiliocosm world-system as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
There are those of the lineages of those who practice by faith and those who practice by dharma—
the eight types of persons— as well as the stream-enterers,
once-returners, non-returners, and arhats.
As for the pratyekabuddhas,
this person, throughout immeasurable kalpas— hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of kalpas—
reverently provided them with robes, bedding, and medicinal requisites.
Furthermore, he gave him all things that were pleasing and fit for enjoyment;
even after his parinirvāṇa, he erected a jeweled stūpa for him.
It is five thousand yojanas high;
its stūpa is adorned with nets of various precious bells.
Throughout the six periods of the day and night, it is entirely [adorned].
One should mentally make offerings to these various stupas and shrines.
If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate,
they will accumulate roots of goodness and the provisions of merit.
It surpasses those merits.

Furthermore, setting aside the beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth throughout the trichiliocosm, and again setting aside the individuals of the stage of faith-following, the stage of dharma-following, and the eight persons within the three thousand worlds; [the merit of this] is even greater.
From those who have attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit, as well as the pratyekabuddhas and so forth,
even unto all the Mahāyāna bodhisattva-mahāsattvas within the trichiliocosm.
And as for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
one should make offerings to them as previously described;
this matter, too, is set aside.
If the cloud-rain-like assemblies throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and as vast as the oceans, filling three thousandfold world-systems,
were all gathered together within a single place of enlightenment,
they would be equal to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are like adamant, as well as to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
This great being reflects and deliberates,
providing various offerings— such as beloved clothing, bedding, food, drink,
and medicinal requisites— to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and tathāgatas.
They made offerings, honored, revered,
and praised [him] for immeasurable years, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of years,
and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
Incalculable kalpas of destruction, incalculable kalpas of formation, and incalculable kalpas of both formation and destruction—
up to as many nayutas of kalpas as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Having already attained the adamantine mind-concentration (*vajracitta-samādhi*),
and [having witnessed] the entry into parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
one constructs stūpas of the seven precious substances, complete with jeweled canopies, bells, and nets.
Even rising as high as the Brahma-world,
if there are men or women who hear this Dharma-gate.
One is able to accumulate the provisions of merit and roots of goodness,
which surpass those previously attained.
Son of the Buddha, I shall now further explain this to you by means of a simile.
By means of this analogy,
those men who are wise and discerning will be able to understand what has been taught;
they will give rise to profound and deep faith and will not engage in disparagement.
Toward such Dharma-preachers who possess understanding,
one should give rise to respect, a sense of wonder, and affection, as if toward the Buddha himself.
Son of the Buddha, it is, for example, as if there were a person.
Within as many three-thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
all sentient beings of the six realms— whether born from an egg, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation— as numerous as the atoms within those Buddha-fields,
as well as those of the lineage of faith-followers, dharma-followers, and the eight types of persons.
From those who have attained the first fruit up to the fourth fruit and the solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas),
as well as those who have accumulated merit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) on the path practiced by the Buddhas,
including all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
They take away their lives and destroy all the stupas.
Furthermore, Son of the Buddha,
there are men who bring sentient beings to maturity, as well as all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
And the accumulation of provisions for the path practiced by all those bodhisattvas,
as well as the meditative concentration on the heart-mantra of the Tathāgata Vajrasamaya and those who have already attained it.
To all the Tathāgatas, Arhats,
Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently residing in the present age,
he makes offerings of flowers, incense, banners, canopies, various flavors, food and drink, and *koṭṭana* (soft) foods, providing every kind of requisite.
And after his parinirvāṇa,
stūpas made of the seven precious jewels were erected,
reaching as high as the Brahma world.
Adorned with canopies, nets, bells, and chimes—
such is the difference between the merit and demerit of these two individuals;
when one considers their ascent and descent, their distance and proximity, and their degree and quantity.
Even throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas of formation and destruction, one cannot find their limit.
O Son of the Buddha,
if there is anyone who hears of such fruits of merit and demerit as these—
One who gives rise to profound and heavy faith in this dharma-gate will,
through the accumulation of all roots of goodness as their provisions,
certainly attain the most supreme state.
One cannot find its limit.
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who slanders this Dharma-gate.
That offense is so great as to be unspeakable;
its limit cannot be reached.
If there is anyone who rejoices in it and accepts it with faith, [the merit shall likewise be immeasurable].
The resulting merit and reward are likewise most vast and great;
they could not be fully described even in eons as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru.
Son of the Buddha, I shall now provide further analogies.
Those who possess wisdom are able to understand and enter this Dharma-gate, thereby attaining great benefit. What is it?
O Son of the Buddha, it is as if there were a person who divided a single hair into one hundred parts,
and with one such part of hair, took up a single drop of water from the great ocean.
What do you think?
Of the two waters, which contains more water:
that which is taken up by the hair, or that which remains?
"Is the water in the ocean more?
Pusiyi replied,
"A drop of water on a single hair is not even worth mentioning."
That which exists within the ocean is exceedingly vast water—
immeasurable, immeasurable.
The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha."
The merit and non-merit that I have spoken of are like water taken up by a hair;
that which I have not yet spoken of is like the water in the great ocean.
It should be understood in this way.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Universal Contemplation of Meaning addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One, although my wisdom is shallow,"
Having heard these teachings on the compliance and contrariety of this Dharma-gate, which bring about great benefit,
I have further reflected upon them and give rise to many doubts;
I pray that you will explain them for me.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent! Ask whatever you wish.
Viśeṣacintin said, "World-Honored One, I see śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."
And other non-Buddhist practitioners such as the Carakas, Parivrājakas, and Nirgranthas;
those of such a kind who either perform asceticism by burning their bodies, or stand on their two feet, or else bend their knees.
They wrap their feet in cloth and sit in a squatting posture;
or they strike two stones together to obtain grain for food;
or they smear their bodies with ash, or throw themselves from high cliffs.
Some lie upon beds of thorns, or enter into great waters and fires;
some eat cow dung, or stand on one leg;
some hold their two arms aloft, or consume only vegetables.
Some eat millet, while others eat tree leaves;
some bathe in cold water, while others enjoy bathing and sporting in the waters of the Ganges.
Such people as these all desire to seek and obtain the Dharma of liberation.
How can such be the karmic retribution for a fool who is stubborn and dull-witted?
World-Honored One, there are those among the administrators and officials who,
giving rise to arrogance, delight in anger, and act with unrestrained self-will, thereby overbearing the power of the foolish.
They are unable to understand the causal relationship between the good and evil karma they perform;
they fail to give what should be given, or give what should not be given,
and they manipulate things to their own liking to exert their influence.
What is the karmic retribution for such categories of people?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, there is another class who likewise practice the life of renunciation together,
yet they are unable to show respect toward those of virtuous conduct and deeds.
He maintains many disciples but does not instruct them at the proper times;
he does not distinguish between what should and should not be done, nor between what constitutes an offense and what does not,
nor between conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Are these worldly dharmas or supramundane dharmas?
Furthermore, he does not understand them himself nor cause others to understand them.
Blessed One, as this karma is accomplished, in which realm will he be reborn?
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
there may be some persons who are unable to show reverence toward their parents, teachers,
and elders, and who do not protect their family or their superiors.
Where will they be reborn?
Furthermore, World-Honored One, there is another class of beings who practice greed, hatred, delusion, and their equal proportions;
where will the karmic retribution of such persons lead them to be reborn?
World-Honored One, there are furthermore the karmas of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
false speech, frivolous speech,
divisive speech, harsh speech, envy, anger, and wrong views.
Where will they be reborn?
Furthermore, there is another class who perform the arts of incantation and spells, not having received them from a teacher but producing these methods through their own delusions;
where will they be reborn?
World-Honored One, there is another class of deluded people who transgress the samaya and perform rites according to their own will;
where will they be reborn?
World-Honored One, as I reflect upon what I have seen and heard,
my mind cannot comprehend it.
I only pray that you will explain it for me, resolving my doubts and bringing about my benefit.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantacintārtha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! and further exclaimed: "Well said!"
"Excellent, excellent, Viśeṣacintin!
Thus he praised him three times:
'For the sake of benefiting and out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world.'"
Furthermore, he expounded upon the causes and conditions of the ultimate principle and the karma of profound depth, posing such questions as these:
"I shall analyze and explain this for you;
you should listen attentively and reflect upon it well."
Viśeṣacintin said,
"I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said to Viśeṣacintin:
If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas,
or various non-Buddhists— such as Carakas, Parivrājakas, or Nirgranthas—
who practice such asceticism of self-immolation by sitting with their feet doubled up and bound with cloth;
The method for making food by striking grain with two stones:
one smears their body with ashes and buries themselves in filth, leaving only the head exposed;
they call this the "Dharma of Liberation."
Some lie upon thorns or cast themselves into deep waters;
some scorch their bodies with the five fires or throw themselves into great conflagrations;
some eat cow dung, constantly stand on one foot, or hold up both arms; others subsist exclusively on vegetables.
Some eat millet or eat tree leaves;
some wash with cold water, enduring the cold in pursuit of purity;
or they bathe in the Ganges while proclaiming it to be liberation.
Those fools, clinging exclusively to their own views as the ultimate truth,
hear his true Dharma and give rise to slander.
I shall now describe the retribution they will receive in the future.
O Son of the Buddha, those who sit squatting while wrapping their garments around themselves will,
upon reaching the Great Lotus Hell,
have their two stones struck together by their own hands as they eat.
They shall be born among camels and donkeys.
If one smears ashes on their body and takes pleasure in practicing the Way [in such a manner],
they shall be born among the Vaiśāsa ghosts who consume vomit.
If one throws oneself from a high cliff,
one will be reborn among the water-rākṣasas.
If one buries one's body in excrement and filth, leaving only the head exposed, and clings to this as being the Way, [one will likewise fall into such states].
They will be born in the great hell of the Forest of Sword-Blades;
if they cast themselves into water seeking liberation,
they will be born within the belly of a great makara fish.
If one scorches one's body with the five fires,
one will fall into the Great Fire Hell;
if one eats cow dung as a means of purification or to counteract poison.
They shall fall into the realm of swine,
where they eat their own excrement;
thereafter, they will again be reborn among the hungry ghosts.
If one stands on tiptoe to recite mantras, taking this to be the Way,
they will become a cauldron-legged yakṣa.
If one raises both arms upward toward the head, taking this to be liberation, [they will likewise fall into error].
One should be reborn as a "hair-standing" hungry ghost;
or, if one eats only vegetables, tree leaves, and weeds,
one will take the body of a camel, a donkey, an elephant, an ox, a sheep, or the like.
If one takes cold water or ice taken from the Ganges River as the path,
one shall fall into the Cold Ice Hell.
Such is the case for those belonging to the class of externalists (tīrthika) who act in this manner.
Holding this to be the true path,
they engage in various karmic actions and are born within the sixteen or thirty-two hells.
Furthermore, there are those who act as overseers.
Whether through power or ignorance,
or through force or shamelessness, they forcibly seize [the property] from one another.
Or one might intend to give this to that person,
yet instead, by exchanging the objects of the gift, one gives them to someone else with a light-hearted alteration of intent.
Or one might give monastic property intended for winter during the summer,
or give property intended for the summer during the winter;
or one might give what was intended to be given promptly at a later time.
Or there may be many things that are quickly exhausted;
all such cases contradict ultimate reality.
After the end of life, one shall be reborn.
Within the sixteen and thirty-two hells,
the physical forms received therein vary according to one's karma; in some cases,
a single body may produce immeasurable heads and faces, each of which is distinct.
Some had the faces of horses, camels, elephants, pigs, weasels;
some had the faces of *cakra* fish, *timi* fish, *māṅga* fish, or *kīla* fish;
some had the faces of *gūḍaśa* fish, cats, wildcats, crows, magpies, or yellow foxes.
Jackal faces, monkey faces, faces of centipedes, faces of centipede-like insects,
water-buffalo faces, bear faces, dragon faces, lion faces, and faces of tigers, wolves, cats, and oxen.
Those with the faces of rabbits, sheep, vultures, and dogs;

those with the parched faces of hungry ghosts (*preta*) and the wrathful faces of *rākṣasas*; and those with the terrifying faces of various evil birds and beasts that strike fear into men—such were the classes of beings, fearsome and exceedingly malevolent.
Those who have multiple heads upon a single body are born as a result of such karma in the Razor-Blade and Sword Hell;
there they move their bodies about, undergoing all manner of suffering.
There is the suffering of extreme pain, the suffering of fierce and cruel torment,
the suffering of savage venom, and the suffering of being deprived of life;
one undergoes these various sufferings until the retribution for one's offenses is fully exhausted.
For that many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas,
in every birth they received bodies in this same manner;
sometimes they had a single head with hundreds of thousands of body parts below it.
Upon each body are hundreds of thousands of billions of heads;
within each head are hundreds of thousands of billions of tongues;
and between each tongue are hundreds of thousands of billions of fiercely blazing flames.
Iron plows and oxen plow their tongues until they are completely worn away.
Thus, each of their hundreds of thousands of millions of bodies contains hundreds of thousands of millions of worms.
They devour their bodies, thirstily drink their blood, and, driven by hunger, eat their flesh.
Tormented by the suffering of hunger and thirst, they tear out their hearts and livers and consume them.
Thus they undergo this retribution for immeasurable years.
After passing through immeasurable kalpas, even up to unspeakably unspeakable billions of nayutas of kalpas,
one will once again be reborn with the body of a sea-rākṣasa.
At times they may pass through eons as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru,
only to be reborn among the hungry ghosts suffering from hunger and thirst;
therein they further pass thirty-six thousand eons among the Śuddhāvāsa deities.
If calculated by human reckoning,
this constitutes unspeakably unspeakable eons since they cast off their bodies from among the hungry ghosts.
When one has taken birth in the bodies of animals— such as camels, donkeys, pigs,
or dogs— for several tens of thousands of years by human calculation,
that constitutes a single day and night in the Saṃghāta Hell.
After passing through hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of years in the hells,
he is born among humans into a family of low caste, despised by others and humiliated by others.
They are born among such families as those of the caṇḍālas, oil-pressers,
and bamboo-workers— families of extreme poverty and suffering.
In every successive life, their bodies constantly suffer from the malignant disease of abdominal dropsy and edema;
they are held in contempt by others,
possessing extremely coarse and hideous forms that are utterly emaciated and frail.
Furthermore, they are excessively greedy for food and never satisfied;
their hands and feet are incomplete, their sense faculties are mostly deficient,
their bodies are mottled and discolored, and their nature is dull and stubborn.
In this way, it becomes increasingly difficult to attain liberation.
Therefore, O Son of the Buddha, you should know that those who manage affairs and various supervisors who do not act according to the Dharma...
When the retribution is received, it will certainly not be in vain;
you must therefore apply your mind and take charge of this matter.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, there is another class of such renunciants.
Arrogant and haughty,
they may be driven by those who hold them in high esteem,
or they may serve as attendants.
Consequently, they become attached to gain, offerings, and fame, and fail to show respect to those of virtuous conduct.
Furthermore, they are unable to perform the duties owed to their preceptors,
nor can they practice the Prātimokṣa vows.
Therefore, one should constantly reflect:
"How may I attain great fame and profit,
surrounded by a retinue of hundreds or thousands?"
If one enters a monastery, a village, a town, a city, a settlement, or a royal capital,
yet is unable to instruct those with whom one dwells or those upon whom one relies,
and furthermore does not explain the light and heavy precepts to them.
Since you yourself do not understand and do not cause others to understand;
since you yourself are not disciplined, tranquil, and secluded,
how can you cause others to be disciplined, tranquil, and secluded?
This is impossible.
One who destroys their own roots of goodness causes others to do likewise;
those who rely upon such a person also destroy their roots of goodness.
Such a person, at the end of life, shall immediately fall together with others into the Pāśa Hell,
where they will transmigrate for one kalpa experiencing suffering,
according to the calculation of days and months by the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
If a human year were equivalent to a full thousand kalpas,
those who dwell together and rely [on such a teacher] would be reborn in the sixteen subsidiary hells and as water-rākṣasas.
They are constantly flogged and have molten copper poured into their mouths.
Son of the Buddha, such a foolish person shall be born in this place.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, there are those who do not accord with or show disrespect toward their parents;
they shall be born among the mynas.
This is the case for those who do not know how to revere their parents and teachers.
One will be born among the loud-voiced camels;
if one treats śramaṇas, brahmins, and others with contempt,
one will be born among the long-necked peacocks.
If there are those who do not respect their parents,
they shall be reborn among the mute, the deaf, pigs, or sheep;
if they engage in greedy, defiled lust, [they shall likewise suffer].
One is born in the three evil realms;
furthermore, if one acts with anger, one will be born among humans with deficient or incomplete sense faculties.
They shall be born in the four realms of existence or in the realm of Yama.
Those who act out of delusion are likewise;
even those with a balanced proportion of the three poisons will receive retributions for their sins as described above, arising without interruption.
A person who takes life shall fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and Yama.
If they are born among humans, they will receive two kinds of retribution.
First, a short lifespan; second, much illness.
If one steals, they will fall into the three miserable realms;
if born among humans, they will experience two kinds of retributive fruits.
First, poverty; second, lack of mastery over shared wealth.
Those who commit sexual misconduct, up to and including those with wrong views, fall into the three evil realms and the realm of Yama.
Those who receive human bodies all experience two kinds of retribution:
first, a short life; second, much illness.
At all places and at all times, they are constantly lacking peace and stability.
O Son of the Buddha, you should clearly understand that such is the karmic retribution for these deeds.
Furthermore, O Son of the Buddha, there is another class of mantra-holders who do not receive the *samaya* precepts from a teacher.
If one performs dhāraṇī-mantras for oneself,
one will then slander the Tathāgatas of the three generations and will be harmed by the Vināyakas.
Furthermore, none of those mantra methods will be accomplished,
and one will incur the sin of falsehood.
This is because, O Son of the Buddha, you have not followed a teacher and do not understand the samaya.
That mantra-practitioner, by thus deceiving both themselves and others,
commits a fraud against all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra (Universally Wise Meaning) [spoke].
Desiring to restate this meaning before the Blessed One,
he spoke in verse: "Subhūti,
whose physical marks are fully perfected, The great rishi-king who holds the mantra without fear."

I prostrate to the Lord of gods and humans, upon whom all rely; Who first mastered the skillful eradication of afflictive habits, And like the moon dispelling darkness, possesses the sovereign, steadfast power of Vajra,
Able to shatter the bonds of enemies and afflictions, And utterly subdue all demonic armies.
The māras of the aggregates, the māra of death, Māra the Lord, and all others— All are subdued and extinguished without remainder;
you have realized the four abodes and the dharmas of fearlessness. Possessing unimpeded liberation, you are named Buddha.
In the past, when you were once a crown prince, You manifested through miraculous birth, free from defilement.
Having first heard this samādhi from the Tathāgata Sūryaprabha-rāja,
he never abandoned his diligence; seeking such a king of samādhis,
he thus encountered successive Buddhas in numbers exceeding the atoms of Mount Sumeru.
With celestial wondrous objects, various incenses, and flowers, he made offerings to the immeasurable Great Teacher.
With a mind of diligent and earnest seeking that never slackened, he vowed to realize and enter samādhi.
He relinquished his own flesh, limbs, hands, and feet, as well as abundant pleasures, playthings, and the throne of kingship.
Constantly providing gifts to the poor and beggars; seeking the Dharma that is difficult to attain even through three samādhis;
serving millions of Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a thousand *sumeru* mountains;
fully cultivating the bodhisattva practices without ever giving rise to a mind of weariness or fatigue—one should always arouse supreme diligence once again.
During the winter season, he practiced austerities, purely observing the prohibitions and all disciplinary rules.
If any offered gifts were misappropriated, or if the timing was altered, or if they were diverted to other monks,
he would cast off his own body to obtain a different body, from which an immeasurable number of heads would emerge.
Each head is like Mount Mīlu; from each grows a long tongue, appearing like a continuous chain of hooks.
Within each head, the tongues are thus; hundreds of koṭis of plows furrow those tongues.
From within each body emerge various worms, numbering as many as the atoms of Mount Mīlu.
Tormented by the burning afflictions of hunger and thirst, they each devour the flesh of their own bodies;
such are the various retributions for their sinful karmas— taking the forms of elephants,
horses, pigs, lions, cats, bears, and monkeys— they prey upon one another’s flesh in turn.
This is the evil retribution for sinful karma: Fierce and raging venomous snakes arise,
along with crows, *khuṅ-hu*, jackals, Dogs, vultures, *kulala*, *gonaśa*,
and other wicked birds, All devouring these sentient beings of evil karma.
Throughout the kalpas of formation and destruction that I have passed through— throughout the countless cycles of formation and decay—
I have devoured sentient beings who committed evil deeds in the Saṃghāta hell, where the trees are exceedingly cruel,
the sword-leaves are fierce and sharp, and the Kālasūtra hell exists; there, cold and heat dismember their limbs and joints.
Those who perform evil deeds are scorched and boiled in the Great Screaming Hell;
the noose of the Black Rope is like a sharp blade, and the same applies to the Black String.
Their bodies and flesh are rotted and ground out, their joints and bones are sawn asunder from top to bottom, and they suffer the agony of being bound and cruelly burned.

Those who commit evil deeds with intense resolve, tormented by the fires of hunger, devour one another and suffer in the Scorching Hell for a full kalpa. For another half-kalpa they fall into the animal realm;
when the kalpa comes to an end, they are born among humans, always in poverty, lowliness, and most wretched places.
Those of inferior lineage and outcaste status (caṇḍāla) shall never be born into noble or superior families;
their bodies will always be mottled with many white leprosy spots.
Due to the retribution of their sins, they may be born among various classes of beings, such as the yakṣas or the realm of hungry ghosts, and shall repeatedly be born into the families of outcasts.
Those who are double-blind, or one-eyed, or deaf and mute;
those with crooked limbs or lameness born of the accumulation of sins; those with stumps for hands or feet, or who are entirely speechless;
those whose minds are inverted and deluded—all these fruits are brought about by karma.
Some are born in the Raurava or Kālasūtra hells;
such various retributions of suffering endure for an entire kalpa or half a kalpa. These fruits arise from the conditions of sinful karma.
If one receives a gift and diverts it elsewhere, or if one diverts a summer offering to the winter portion, [the same retribution follows].
Driven by these karmic actions, they are born among the eight difficult states; within those various difficulties, they are subjected to extreme severity.
They are also born with sixteen types of kinsmen, scorched and boiled by manifold sufferings that are most terrifying.
Their forms and appearances number eighteen or twenty, all receiving evil retributions due to the conditions of their karma.
If one gives rise to a mind of contempt toward one's parents, Or fails to respect elders and those of venerable lineage, After the end of life, one will fall among animals;
Among various flying birds such as the starling, One will be neither honored above, below, nor in the middle. At the end of life, one is born among animals.
Or one may be born among peacocks with long necks;

having failed to provide filial support or respect for one's parents, and having shown no reverence toward those of national virtue or elders, after the end of life one is reborn among animals as a loud-voiced camel or a donkey.
This is the case for whoever treats their parents with contempt.
They fall among pigs and donkeys, feeding on impurities;
yet those wise and intelligent ones who have realized the near and far shores of birth and death should honor and respect their parents as the supreme field of merit,
being born into wealthy families of right faith.
If one treats with contempt those of virtuous deeds, the devas who protect the Dharma will abandon them;
malevolent spirits and ghosts will find their opportunity, and hosts of yakṣas will come to terrify them.
If one treats with contempt one’s parents, one will always dwell in a poor household throughout every lifetime.
At all times one will suffer contempt and humiliation, And be reborn among the dull-witted and servile.
If one treats one's parents with disrespect, One will never find even a moment of peace and happiness;
Wife, children, and kinsmen will all be distressed, And there will be no food or drink to satisfy one’s hunger.
Even if the entire nation were to feed them, it would never suffice; they take birth in the form of hungry ghosts as an extremely evil retribution.
If one treats one’s parents with contempt, one will surely be born as a sea-rākṣasa, whose body blazes like a fierce flame, constantly consuming molten iron throughout day and night.

Those who treat their parents with contempt, And those who show disdain for elders and the virtuous, Are constantly loathed and shunned by the world; The same holds true for their wives and concubines.
Such various types of evil beings— To describe them would not be exhausted even in an eon.
If one does not commit transgressions against the Venerable One, they are called a wise and intelligent person;
the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion do not arise, and their physical, verbal, and mental actions are always at peace.
If, however, with an angry and evil mind one takes the life of a living being, one will fall into the four miserable realms and suffer for a long time.
Stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying; Harsh speech, double-tongued speech, and idle chatter;
The various karmic fruits of greed, anger, and delusion— One shall never obtain human happiness through these.
If one gives wealth and treasures with a pure mind, One should always guard and be cautious regarding all precepts and actions.
Cultivating patience without regression, with diligence and without indolence, they enter meditative concentration;
through the mirror of prajñā, they are always detached. Such a person shall surely attain sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and will never commit sexual misconduct;
they will always remain far removed from faults of speech and mind.
Thus you shall become a Great Guide, expounding the True Dharma for all sentient beings;
with not even a moment’s thought of anger, you will be freed from the bonds of Māra and false views.
Before long, you shall become a lamp for the world, transforming all through the bright Dharma of the ten wholesome paths.
Those who steal and hold wrong views, those who will be born in the future as "needle-mouthed" insects,
those of malicious intent who use frivolous speech and double-tongued talk to constantly destroy right view,
and those who practice the teachings of external paths by throwing themselves from high cliffs or lying upon beds of thorns— [all these shall suffer].
One who gives wealth and goods with such wrong views will receive only a meager reward of material sustenance;
however, one who gives to those practicing the correct path will surely obtain an inexhaustible and great fruit.
If you wish to accomplish the three sites of enlightenment, you must all receive instruction by studying under a teacher.
Those who do not follow the instructions, performing rites in vain and lacking reality,
because they do not respect the Teacher, will be unable to practice the maṇḍala.
If one desires the supreme [attainment] through the most excellent, within the true Dharma of the Great Universal Assembly Sūtra, [one must act accordingly].
The most supreme and vast field within the three realms,
The noble ones of the Vajra family— the maṇi jewel, the lotus, and the white elephant—
Within which all Buddhas exercise sovereign mastery over the most excellent and sublime Dharma-jewels; O Candraśekhara-vajramukuṭa!
The Jewel Garland, the Sunlight Garland, the Dharma-Crown Maṇi, and the Universal Crown—all these enter into the Vajra Garland.
One should constantly recite these protective dhāraṇīs without interruption;
with every thought, one is able to extinguish karmic obstacles.
Reciting the mantra continuously during the three periods of day and night,
one will certainly benefit without doubt. Whether staying in a high place, on the banks of a river, at various shrines of the gods,
in excellent and wondrous locations, in the wilds, among graves, or in places of profound tranquility, one shall certainly always subsist on alms.
By this, one accomplishes the maṇḍala; according to the instructions and as taught, by following the essential path, one attains correspondence with that true meaning.
One will certainly achieve the great principles and the thirty-two kinds of accomplishments, having attained the dharma of the true site through upholding [the teachings].
This is called the essential practice for accomplishment without impairment;
it is the completion of one hundred *homā* and *pūjā* rites within the three types of maṇḍalas.
Through this, the supreme maṇḍala is accomplished, free from doubt and certain; one shall always maintain deep faith in this most excellent Dharma.
Be careful never to recite the Citta-mantra, nor pay homage to various malevolent deities.
If one does not worship other worldly spirits, one may construct the three types of maṇḍalas.
Furthermore, one should always refrain from harming the lives of others and never destroy the minds of others.
Because one has distanced oneself from spells that possess people, one will then be able to accomplish the maṇḍala.

However, if one uses clothing made of black sheep wool, consumes unwholesome food, or acts with a malicious intent to cause harm, the recitation of various mantras and all performed mantra-rites will fail to succeed;
one will immediately fall away and lose the accomplishment of the mantra-methods.

One who constantly protects that vajra and does not consume sesame, flowers, cakes, and the like, the wise one should perform the supreme mantra; this ritual method and its meaning shall be accomplished.
If one does not accept the teacher’s instruction, the vināyakas will swiftly seize them.

If one can receive the empowerment from a master and have the crown of one's head consecrated by all the Tathāgatas, one will not harm others nor be possessed by malevolent spirits; this is called the "Threefold Maṇḍala.
The wise explain its principle with a humble mind, maintaining equanimity toward those of high and low status alike.
One who has attained true accomplishment in all worlds through the equality of the true mantra,
yet speaks falsely among many people, traveling east, west, south, and north,
such that their undertakings are not successful and their activities do not accord with their wishes— such a person should not be said to have accomplished the mantra.
Those of meager merit give rise to calamities and are harmed by *vināyakas*;
if one can accomplish the rite of painting [an image] with mantras, and burns incense and offers lamps according to the Dharma, such is the category of those who have accomplished the mantra-rites;
all of these are brought about through the power of compassionate action.
First is the accomplishment of the karma of non-killing.
Those who possess compassion and pity, being true practitioners, shall invoke the various mantra-kings from the ten directions.
Clearly proclaiming the definitive and actual benefits, one should practice this with all ritual implements in their essential reality, as cultivated by all mantra-holders.
Those mantra-practitioners who possess wisdom should accomplish the maṇḍala of the auspicious abode of the Thirty-three Gods;
by means of the three types of samaya equal to my own,
they shall accomplish the various mantra-dharmas, the power of whose merit is unspeakable.
If there is one who performs the foremost rite, according to the principles explained in the maṇḍala,
they shall accomplish the ritual through their pure faith; by being in union with the three samādhis and using vidyā-mantras,
they shall destroy the triple world, and all mantras within the triple world shall be accomplished.
Exerting oneself with diligent application, one should further increase the practice; all the mantra rites performed will then be accomplished.
One should draw the form of a vajra and the characteristics of a lotus upon a maṇḍala in an open space, using colored powders and precious gems to delineate the boundary lines.
If a wise person accomplishes this according to the Dharma, it is called the truly authentic and vastly beneficial painted maṇḍala.
One does not paint a vajra, nor the forms of Buddhas or their sons (bodhisattvas),
nor mantra-holders, cetas, cetikas, vināyakas, or messengers.
Duṭa duṭi kiṃkara; one should draw these all before the image according to one's capacity, with reverence and faith.
Offer as many of these to the Supreme Guides, and bestow the finest flavors upon Ceṭas and others, as well as Piśācas, so that they may be delighted.
The mantra-holding ṛṣis should prepare offerings before an accomplished image of the Buddha made according to the Dharma;
they should all be drawn within that maṇḍala and installed before the Buddha in accordance with the ritual.
At the various doors of the practice hall, images of Vināyakas should be painted.
One should paint the guardian deities of the locality; furthermore, one should paint the mountain-dwelling mantra-holding ṛṣis, all standing with palms joined before the Buddha.
In this manner, there are twenty-eight mantra-deities, seven depicted on each side.
One should also depict the forms of the sun and moon deities and the forms of the mantra-deities.
To protect and sustain the practitioner and bring them to accomplishment: on the eastern side, depict Indra;
on the southern side, depict Uśīra; on the western side, depict the Mountain of Sunset (Asta);
and on the northern side, depict Gandhamādana. On all these mountains, depict the seats of the mantra-siddhas.
With palms joined, he stands before the Buddha image; with his neck bound by chains, he stays before the great seer who upholds the mantra.
His hands are entwined as a messenger holding an iron chain, manifesting a sign of disturbance toward the ritual of the mantra. There are thirty-two kinnaras.
On each side there are eight [deities]; within the pure mandala, their forms are drawn.

If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the Buddha-maṇḍala, it should be adorned with a thousand lamps and a thousand flowers, along with a thousand incense vases and various offerings, as well as the flute, lute, harp, and *vīṇā*.
Sheng, di, xiao, drums, and all manner of music; long flutes, gongs, and various musical instruments—those devas who delight in such sounds come before the Buddha image to strike and beat them.
Furthermore, they spread various kinds of jeweled nets and display various wondrous colors and realms.
Various jeweled vases offered like clouds can accomplish the supreme and wondrous dharma of the maṇḍala.
However, if it is seized by a vināyaka, that person will ultimately not accomplish the supreme dharma;
the power of all mantras will swiftly perish, and the efficacy of diligent practice will likewise fail to be realized.
Those who do not practice the various meditative concentrations and abandon cultivation, yet seek accomplishment at a superior maṇḍala—
such foolish people performing these rites will never achieve the supreme benefit.
If one can act according to the instructions for the maṇḍala rite, having already fulfilled it for twelve years, [one shall succeed].
Dedicate yourself exclusively to the recitation and upholding of the mantra, performing no other activity.
On high precipices or in pure locations, one can extinguish all sins through the power of the mantra.
When desiring to recite the mantra or at the site of the mandala, always use non-glutinous rice, milk, curd, and so forth; recite during three periods each day and night.
When reciting, exert all one's strength to reach the prescribed number of repetitions;
on the eighth, fifteenth, and full moon days, practice by constructing a maṇḍala. One will certainly attain supreme accomplishment.
For those who contemplate with analytical discernment, this is the Sūtra of the Most Victorious Principle.
Dig one zhang into the earth and take pure soil; use this mud to purify the ground and construct the altar according to the ritual.

Having bathed for purification and donned clean robes, with a sincere mind and focused mindfulness, recite [the mantra] over three or four cubits, or seven times seven cubits. Take fine, pure soil to create the purified altar.
One should request the Mahāyāna Sūtra of Sublime Victory; by performing this rite, one will obtain great benefit.
This is the section on the practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna-Vajracūḍamaṇi.
